transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-21 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Samir Khan (Redwood AE), Jules Ortega (Redwood SE), Lina Park (Redwood CSM), Maya Patel (VantageHealth VP Eng), Noah Green (VantageHealth SRE), Sasha Ivanov (VantageHealth Product)

Summary:
Quick debrief of the 12/15 latency surge and customer experience impact, agreed-to mitigations (short and medium term), workshoped escape-hatch routing and runbook rehearsal plan, and agreed next steps to accelerate pilot and prevent recurrence.

Topics:
- Incident timeline and likely root causes (KV cache TTL + autoscaler bump + cold-prime penalty)
- Immediate mitigations (prefix caching, canary fallback, rate limiting)
- Long-term reliability items (escape-hatch routing, dedicated capacity pilot, observability gaps)
- Security/compliance notes (audit logs, data retention for traces)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Samir: alright hey everyone thanks for joining, we'll kick off in a minute, couple of goals for today are to close the RCA, make a concrete runbook rehearsal plan and then workshop the escape-hatch so you can move faster into a pilot. sound good?
[00:12] Maya: yep that sounds good, thanks Samir. good to have Lina here too.
[00:15] Noah: hi all, I'm mostly here for the SRE detail — want to make sure we capture traces.
[00:20] Jules: hey, gonna share my screen with the timeline and a few latency heatmaps, hope that's ok — there's a small chance the transcription messes up model names so i'll also drop links in the doc.
[00:30] Sasha: fine by me. quick ask — when you say "escape-hatch" what exactly do you mean? like immediate switch to smaller model or a different region?
[00:38] Samir: good question — escape-hatch is a policy we propose: when end-to-end P95 hits X and error rate Y, automatically route to a lower-cost variant that uses cached prefixes and smaller KV cache retention, or route to dedicated pool if reserved; it's about preserving core UX while shedding load.
[00:57] Maya: okay so it's not just "throw to smaller model" — it's a controlled policy with cache-aware routing. good.
[01:05] Jules: right, and practically we have two levers: model-variant routing and infra-tier routing. model variants keep the same host but change quantization/batching profile; infra-tier routing moves requests to dedicated capacity or to a different region. both have cost/latency tradeoffs.
[01:25] Noah: during the 12/15 event we saw a compounding problem: a short spike in traffic triggered autoscalerbacks — um autoscaler thrash? — which then led to more cold starts and a cascade where more KV cache misses happened. once KV miss rate spiked, latency climbed nonlinearly.
[01:46] Jules: yep, the KV cache TTL config was tuned for typical loads, not the kind of fanout you had. cache churn + concurrent GC-ish behavior caused an extra serialization path that added 150-300ms per request at high QPS.
[02:05] Maya: hmm we thought the cache would handle it, that surprised us. is that something Redwood can tune or is it us?
[02:12] Jules: it's a bit of both — config is on the Redwood side, but the workload shape (bursty clinical ingestion around midnight) is on yours. we suggested, in the quick post-incident notes, a larger prefix cache for those endpoints plus a small TTL bump. but that alone doesn't fix the autoscaler thrash.
[02:30] Samir: to be clear, we ran a repro in staging yesterday where we drove load around your pattern and reproduced the increase in KV misses. we have traces that show the exact path. I've linked them — will circulate.
[02:40] Noah: good. can we get the raw traces? we want to join them with our ingress logs and the downstream DB times.
[02:45] Jules: yes, action item for me — i'll upload the 10-minute slices around the incident with the annotated spans.
[02:50] Lina: quick ops-centric note: customer experience was degraded by about seven minutes of tail latency spikes, but error rate only bumped for two endpoints. overall your users saw slow responses which created retries and magnified the load. the mitigation we used that helped was a manual rate-switch and temporary quota — folks, remember this was manual.
[03:12] Maya: right, and that manual step is exactly what we want to avoid — hence the escape-hatch conversation.
[03:20] Sasha: product question — are you recommending dedicated capacity for the whole service or just for the three critical endpoints?
[03:27] Jules: we recommend a hybrid: dedicated pool for critical endpoints (the ones you called out in the doc), hosted for the rest. that keeps cost manageable while giving isolation for the SLA-critical paths.
[03:35] Noah: cost question — what's the delta in monthly cost to reserve dedicated for three endpoints at our QPS?
[03:40] Samir: approximate first-pass number i'll pull from the pricing grid — short answer: not insignificant but within the runway if those endpoints drive revenue; we'll send a detailed estimate as a follow-up.
[03:50] Maya: request: include a sensitivity band in the estimate for 20-50% traffic growth.
[03:55] Samir: yep will do.
[04:00] Jules: back to the technical mitigations — short-term we can do: prefix-level caching (bump prefix cache to hold hot keys), slightly increase KV TTL, add a short-lived token-bucket throttle on non-critical routes, and implement an automatic model-variant fallback at the router level.
[04:20] Noah: about model-variant fallback, are we talking quantization or smaller context length?
[04:24] Jules: mostly quantization + smaller context. quantized variants give faster execution and smaller memory footprint; also we can enable aggressive KV cache sharing for the smaller model so hit-rate improves. downsides are marginally lower quality and a change in hallucination profile — we'll tie that to an eval set.
[04:42] Sasha: productly, we'll accept slight quality difference only if we can guarantee no data leak and predictable SLA.
[04:48] Lina: on the security side — customer asked about audit logs and data retention for the traces we'll share. Samir, you said Redwood can provide redacted traces and encrypted exports?
[04:56] Samir: yes, we can provide trace exports with PII redaction and KMS-encrypted bundles. we log model names and route IDs but can mask user payload. we also have SOC2 artifacts and ISO alignment documents; we'll attach the security pack in the follow-up.
[05:12] Maya: need the exact retention policy on logs for compliance — our legal team will ask.
[05:18] Samir: noted. Lina will include the retention matrix in the postmortem packet.
[05:22] Lina: yes, i'll include a simple table: trace retention 90 days by default, audit logs 1 year — but we can extend on enterprise.
[05:30] Noah: we also need a permanent route for 72-hour detailed trace retention for incidents, separate from the default.
[05:36] Jules: doable as an opt-in. we'll add that to the proposal.
[05:40] Maya: ok good.
[05:42] [10:00] (screen sharing briefly omitted in transcript)
[10:05] Jules: showing the heatmap now — see the spike around 23:42 UTC on 12/15, and notice how KV miss-rate correlates with the jump in p99. you can also see garbage-collection-ish pauses when we scaled down nodes too quickly.
[10:25] Noah: that scaling policy is aggressive on our side — we wanted to save cost. maybe we under-provisioned the minimum replicas.
[10:32] Jules: yes, there's a knob on min replicas that would have prevented the cold-start spiral. that's a config change we can recommend you make today and roll out in the next maintenance window.
[10:44] Samir: suggested immediate config change: increase min replicas by 30% for the three critical routes during your peak window. that's reversible.
[10:52] Maya: can you put exact numbers in a PR so my infra team can review?
[10:56] Samir: yes, jules will prepare the PR with exact values.
[11:02] Sasha: what about the observability gaps — we found traces but correlating them with the upstream gateway was manual. can Redwood provide a single trace id mapping?
[11:10] Jules: we can generate a crosswalk id and add a small header in the request that propagates across your ingress, which makes joins much easier. it's a minor instrumentation change.
[11:20] Noah: please do that; that'll speed postmortems.
[11:24] Samir: okay added as an action item for jules.
[11:30] Lina: next bit is the runbook rehearsal — we recommend a 60-min tabletop where we simulate a 3x load spike, run the automated escape-hatch policy in a canary and measure recovery. who should attend?
[11:42] Maya: our SREs (Noah + one other), our product lead (Sasha), and infra engineer (TBD) — we'll nominate names by 12/24.
[11:52] Samir: Redwood will bring a play-by-play facilitator; lina will run the runbook doc, jules will execute the canary config. goal: validate we can go from detection to quarantine in under 2 minutes.
[12:00] Noah: under 2 minutes is aggressive but worth aiming for. what are the detection mechanisms?
[12:05] Jules: we'll use adaptive latency monitors (p95/p99 thresholds) + request error-rate spike detector; combined signals will flip the router to the variant. detection window can be tuned — start at 60s.
[12:18] Maya: and we need a manual override path in case auto-fallback misfires.
[12:22] Samir: agreed, manual override included and also a step to rollback within 15 minutes if quality regressions observed.
[12:30] Sasha: timeline question — if we go forward with dedicated pilot what's the fastest we can get it live?
[12:36] Samir: with a priority pilot we can stand up a dedicated pool in 3 weeks, assuming contract/commitment signed; engineering side can be a week once infra is provisioned.
[12:45] Maya: procurement will need the pricing + commitment options. please include an option for short-term burst instead of full reserved for 90 days.
[12:52] Samir: will add that variant.
[13:00] Jules: one more thing on root cause — there's a subtle interaction with our batching heuristics. in high concurrency the batching window shrinks and can increase tail latency although average throughput looks fine. we need to adjust batching thresholds for your workload.
[13:12] Noah: makes sense. add that to the repro and test plan.
[13:18] Jules: done.
[13:22] [45:00] (group discussion about labelling and documentation)
[45:05] Lina: recap — we have a short-term checklist (increase min replicas for critical routes, bump prefix cache, enable header crosswalk, implement token-bucket throttling for non-critical routes) and a medium-term plan (escape-hatch automation, dedicated pool pilot, runbook rehearsal).
[45:25] Maya: yes and the deliverables + owners are clear. I also want the security docs and retention matrix.
[45:33] Samir: i'll include the security pack and a redact sample for traces.
[45:38] Noah: my ask — please include an ingest sample so we can test locally.
[45:42] Jules: will do.
[45:45] Sasha: final question — competitor lock-in concerns: how do we avoid being stuck if we later switch providers?
[45:51] Samir: we publish model metadata and the router config; exports are standard and we can help with migration playbooks. we can also contractually commit to data portability clauses.
[46:05] Maya: ok that's reassuring.
[46:08] Lina: any other questions?
[46:12] (silence)
[46:15] Samir: if not, quick recap of next steps and i'll call out owners. (recap) Samir to send RCA deck and link to traces by 12/23; Jules to do KV retention tests + trace upload by 12/28; Noah to upload ingress extracts by 12/22; Maya to confirm list of critical endpoints and SLAs by 12/24; Lina to schedule runbook rehearsal for week of 1/4 and share invite by 12/30; Redwood eng to prototype escape-hatch config by 1/5.
[46:55] Maya: thanks folks, appreciate the focus and the clear plan.
[47:00] Noah: thanks.
[47:03] Sasha: thanks everyone.
[47:05] Samir: thanks, we'll follow up in writing after this call.

End of transcript.
